extracted.intended_audience: startup founders / early-stage founders seeking media coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for founders on how to get press coverage for startups by building journalist relationships, crafting newsworthy stories, and pitching effectively over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold emails don't work
rubrics_metrics.description: Cold outreach is ineffective because journalists are extremely busy and inundated with pitches; a single cold email is likely to get lost in the shuffle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists produce multiple stories per day, run social media, chase breaking news, fact-check, and answer editors — they receive pitches daily. If your strategy relies on cold outreach, rethink it: successful press coverage is about building relationships over time. Action: reflect on current PR strategy and move away from mass cold-emailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build the relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate media relationships before you pitch by following journalists and engaging with their content; media relationships are a long game, like planting a garden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow journalists on Twitter and LinkedIn, comment on their posts, share their articles, and add thoughtful insights (not flattery). Think in terms of months, not weeks — you're building social capital. Action item: choose three journalists who regularly cover your industry, follow them, and engage meaningfully at least once a week for the next three months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer value; be a resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Position yourself as a helpful source of expertise and fresh perspective rather than someone always asking for coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer help from the perspective of who you are (e.g., 'I have a lot of perspective on Fintech startups in Southeast Asia'). Do homework on what each journalist covers so your offer aligns with their beats. Use tools (the article suggests AI tools like Perplexity) to research and tailor your outreach. Action item: draft a short, friendly quarterly template focused on how you can help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research journalists' beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Do specific research into the kinds of stories each journalist typically covers so you can tailor your offers and pitches to their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research tools (example: Perplexity) to learn a journalist's typical coverage and craft outreach that aligns with their interests and beats. Tailored offers make you a more useful resource and improve chances of getting coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch a story that readers will find interesting (not just company news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pitching company-centric milestones ('We just raised a round', 'We just hired a CTO', 'We just launched a product'); instead pitch insights, trends, or unique angles that provide value to the journalist's audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good story examples: 'Our data shows that user behavior is changing in a big way'; 'The market for our product was tiny when we first launched, but now it’s huge (and here’s why)'; 'We came up with an insanely unique way to grow.' These are audience-facing and insightful. Contrast these with the uninteresting examples to judge newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft an irresistible pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with a warm relationship and a great story, the pitch must be concise, timely, relevant, and clearly communicate why the journalist's readers will care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: a clear, attention-grabbing subject line; a brief introduction reminding the journalist how you know each other; the core of your story in two sentences; and reasons their readers will love the story. Be concise but provide enough detail to pique interest. Before sending, ask: Is this story truly newsworthy? Does it align with the journalist's usual coverage? Will readers love this story?

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider offering exclusives
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering an exclusive to a single journalist can be particularly effective because it gives them a chance to break the news and more time to research and write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exclusive can increase a journalist's interest and provide them time to prepare a stronger piece, rather than forcing a rushed story. Use strategically when the story is strong and timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use templates and cadence for outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a planned cadence for outreach and use short, friendly templates focused on offering help rather than asking for coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends drafting a template to send out quarterly. Keep templates concise, focused on how you can help, and update them based on the journalist's recent work so they remain relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think long-term; be patient
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting press is a marathon, not a silver bullet; the objective is to become a trusted voice journalists turn to for insights, not to secure a single mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start implementing relationship-building strategies before you have news. Over time, consistent engagement and offering value will increase the likelihood journalists consider your stories. Patience and persistence are key.
